key_points.text: A problem can be solved by computational methods if it can be broken down and solved by an algorithm in a finite number of steps, using decomposition, abstraction, calculation and stored data, in a reasonable time with the resources available.

Problem recognition: from a scenario, identify what the actual problem is. Then decompose it into smaller sub-problems and use abstraction to remove details that don't matter, before designing a solution.

Divide and conquer repeatedly splits a problem into smaller ones of the same kind (binary search halves the data each time; merge sort and quick sort split, sort and combine). Parts may also be done at the same time.

Backtracking tries one path at a time and, at a dead end, goes back to the last decision to try another option, as when solving a maze or traversing a tree depth first. Read, trace and write code that uses it.
Data mining searches large data sets for previously unknown patterns, for example shopping habits or fraud. It can find useful insights, but it needs a lot of processing and raises privacy concerns.
Heuristics give a good-enough answer quickly when an exact answer would take too long, as with A*'s estimated distance to the goal. Trade-off: speed over guaranteed accuracy.

Performance modelling predicts how a system will behave (such as under heavy load) using models or simulations, so problems are found before building or testing the real thing, which might be costly, dangerous or impossible.

Pipelining (problem solving): the output of one process feeds into the next, so several stages work at once on different items. Visualisation presents data or a design graphically, to spot patterns or build a mental model of what a program will do and plan ahead.

dont_confuse.text: Divide and conquer vs decomposition: decomposition breaks a problem into different sub-tasks; divide and conquer splits it into smaller versions of the same problem.
Pipelining in 2.2.2 vs 1.1.1: the same idea (output of one stage feeds the next while other stages work on other items), applied to processes in a program rather than the stages of the FDE cycle.
Heuristic vs algorithm: an algorithm follows exact steps to a correct answer; a heuristic is a shortcut that gives a good-enough answer faster.
